passage:
The received account of minimalist music casts it as a principled assault on the expressive surplus of late Romanticism: by stripping melody down to repeated cells, by emptying harmony of tonal drama, composers such as Philip Glass and Steve Reich are said to have evacuated the very subjectivity that European concert music had spent three centuries elaborating. Plausible as this narrative sounds, it rests on a confusion between surface austerity and genuine asceticism — a confusion that dissolves once one attends to what minimalism actually does to the listener's experience rather than to what it withholds from the score.

The key to a fuller reading lies in what theorists of perception have called the figure-ground relation. In conventionally structured tonal music, melody functions as figure against a harmonic ground; the listener's attention is continuously solicited by the melody's forward motion. Minimalism inverts this hierarchy without abolishing it. The repeated pattern — what Glass called the "pulsing lattice" — recedes to become ground, and from that ground emergent figures arise not in the score but in the listener's nervous system: phantom melodies, illusory accelerations, fleeting tonal centers that no performer has played. Far from evacuating subjectivity, the minimalist text converts the listener from a passive recipient of compositional intention into an involuntary co-author of the sonic event. The experience is less akin to watching a painting than to standing inside a loom — one perceives not a finished image but a process that one's own perceptual apparatus completes, differently each time.

This account complicates the familiar opposition between minimalism and expression. Critics who charge the style with emotional vacancy typically measure emotional content by its legibility: a crescendo is readable, a sforzando communicable, a Romantic cadence cathartic in a way that an ostinato cycling through seven minutes of eighth notes is not. But legibility is not equivalent to depth. What minimalism sacrifices is emotional pre-packaging — the composer's prior decision about what the listener should feel and when. What it preserves, and indeed intensifies, is the phenomenological density of musical time: time that presses, that accumulates without resolving, that forces an unprecedented awareness of duration itself as aesthetic content. This is not the attenuated emotion of a music that has given up; it is the demanding emotion of a music that has given responsibility away.

To appreciate the full stakes of this distinction, one need only consider how minimalism's procedures have been appropriated — and thereby misread — by commercial ambient music. Where Glass or Reich constructs a lattice designed to activate emergent perception, commercial ambient composition produces stasis for consumption: background that demands nothing, offers nothing unexpected, and vanishes from memory the moment the speakers fall silent. The superficial resemblance — repetition, slow harmonic rhythm, unmarked dynamics — has led many listeners to conflate the two, but the distinction is phenomenologically decisive. Minimalism is arduous precisely because it withholds the interpretive scaffolding the listener has come to expect; ambient music is effortless precisely because it erects a simulacrum of that scaffolding while providing none of its structural load. The confusion, in short, is between a music that asks the listener to build and a music that offers a ready-made ruin.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Minimalist music, by eliminating harmonic complexity, successfully overcame the emotional excesses characteristic of late Romantic orchestral composition.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The standard account of minimalism as emotionally vacant misunderstands its workings, because minimalism relocates rather than eliminates subjectivity by activating emergent perception in the listener.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Philip Glass and Steve Reich should be credited with transforming the listener from a passive audience member into an active co-author of musical experience.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Commercial ambient music, by imitating minimalism's surface features without replicating its structural demands, has misled critics into condemning minimalism as emotionally empty.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The figure-ground relation, borrowed from perceptual psychology, provides the best available framework for analyzing the emotional content of any genre of contemporary music.

explanations.correct: The passage's thesis, introduced at the end of paragraph 1 and developed across all four paragraphs, is that the received account of minimalism as an evacuation of subjectivity is wrong: minimalism relocates subjectivity into the listener's perceptual activity rather than eliminating it. B integrates both the rejection of the standard view and the author's positive account.
explanations.A: This paraphrases the received account the passage explicitly rejects — it is the view the author argues against, not the author's own conclusion.
explanations.B: Correct. This captures both the adversative move (standard account is wrong) and the substantive claim (subjectivity is relocated, not eliminated).
explanations.C: Too narrow: this states only one strand of the argument (paragraph 2) without the overarching challenge to the received account or the distinction from ambient music.
explanations.D: This describes the final paragraph's point, not the overall thesis; it also misidentifies the causal chain — critics condemn minimalism for reasons the passage traces to misunderstanding of its mechanisms, not solely to conflation with ambient music.
explanations.E: The figure-ground relation is introduced as a key conceptual tool in paragraph 2 but is not the passage's main claim; the passage does not argue the concept applies to all contemporary music genres.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward critics who charge minimalism with emotional vacancy can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: dismissive contempt for a view that has been conclusively refuted by experimental research in auditory perception

choices.label: B
choices.text: qualified sympathy, in that the critics correctly identify a surface feature of minimalism while drawing an unwarranted conclusion from it

choices.label: C
choices.text: reluctant agreement that minimalism sacrifices communicable emotion even if it gains in phenomenological complexity

choices.label: D
choices.text: measured disagreement, conceding that the critics' standard of legibility has some merit but arguing that it is an insufficient measure of emotional depth

choices.label: E
choices.text: undisguised admiration for critics who prioritize the communicable and legible over the merely structural in musical aesthetics

explanations.correct: In paragraph 3 the author grants that a crescendo or Romantic cadence is legible and cathartic in ways an ostinato is not, before arguing that 'legibility is not equivalent to depth.' This concessive structure — granting the critics a point, then reframing its significance — is precisely measured disagreement with a concession.
explanations.A: The author does not invoke experimental research and is not contemptuous; the tone is analytical and concessive before it is adversarial.
explanations.B: The critics do not correctly identify a 'surface feature' so much as correctly identify a real difference in legibility; more importantly, the author does not express sympathy — the author's stance is disagreement, not sympathy.
explanations.C: The author explicitly denies that minimalism sacrifices emotion; rather, it sacrifices 'emotional pre-packaging,' which is a different claim.
explanations.D: Correct. The author concedes the legibility point and then reframes it as an insufficient standard — exactly measured disagreement with a concession.
explanations.E: The author does not admire the critics; the passage's argumentative arc is aimed at correcting their view.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A received view is introduced and immediately rejected; a perceptual framework is then offered to replace it; the framework is applied to distinguish minimalism from a superficially similar genre.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two competing theories of musical emotion are introduced and compared; experimental evidence for each is weighed; a synthesis incorporating both is proposed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A biographical account of two minimalist composers is offered; their techniques are described in detail; the broader cultural significance of those techniques is assessed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A critique of late Romanticism is developed; minimalism is presented as its corrective; the limitations of minimalism are then acknowledged and partially defended.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A received view is introduced; a fuller account is developed across two paragraphs; a potential objection from ambient music's defenders is anticipated and dismissed.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces and challenges the received narrative. Paragraph 2 introduces the figure-ground framework as the basis for a fuller account. Paragraph 3 applies this to rebut the emotional-vacancy charge. Paragraph 4 uses the framework to distinguish minimalism from commercial ambient music. A captures all three moves accurately.
explanations.A: Correct. The sequence — received view challenged, perceptual framework offered, framework applied to distinguish minimalism from ambient music — matches the passage's four-paragraph arc.
explanations.B: The passage does not weigh experimental evidence for competing theories; it offers a single analytic framework and applies it. No synthesis of two theories is proposed.
explanations.C: The passage is not biographical; Glass and Reich are mentioned only briefly, and no biographical detail is provided. The focus is on musical procedures and listener experience.
explanations.D: The passage is not a critique of late Romanticism; Romanticism is mentioned only as backdrop. More importantly, the passage does not acknowledge and defend limitations of minimalism — it defends minimalism throughout.
explanations.E: The final paragraph is not primarily about anticipating and dismissing an objection from ambient music's defenders; it is about using the distinction to clarify what minimalism actually does. Also, paragraph 3's content is omitted in E's summary.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, what does the author mean by describing minimalism as a music that has "given responsibility away"?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Minimalist composers have abandoned their duty to communicate specific emotional content to the listener, resulting in works that are aesthetically incomplete.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Minimalist composers have transferred to the listener the task of determining what emotional experience the music will produce, thereby intensifying phenomenological engagement.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Minimalist composers have delegated compositional decisions to performers, who must improvise within the constraints of the repeating pattern.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Minimalist composers have ceded aesthetic authority to commercial interests, allowing the style to be appropriated by the ambient music industry.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Minimalist composers have rejected the responsibility of building on prior musical traditions, producing works that are historically irresponsible.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 states that what minimalism 'preserves, and indeed intensifies, is the phenomenological density of musical time,' and that it is 'the demanding emotion of a music that has given responsibility away' — meaning the responsibility for emotional pre-packaging has been transferred from composer to listener. B captures this precisely.
explanations.A: The author does not say the works are aesthetically incomplete; the passage argues the opposite — that minimalism's emotional content is deep, not absent.
explanations.B: Correct. The passage identifies 'emotional pre-packaging' as what minimalism sacrifices — the composer's prior decision about what to feel — transferring that work to the listener.
explanations.C: The passage does not discuss performers or improvisation; the figure-ground account concerns the listener's perceptual activity, not a performer's interpretive latitude.
explanations.D: This conflates the argument of paragraph 4 (ambient music appropriates minimalism) with the phrase in paragraph 3, which concerns the composer-listener relationship, not commerce.
explanations.E: The passage nowhere implies minimalism is historically irresponsible; this imports a judgment absent from the text.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following claims about emergent perception in minimalist music?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a wholly unconscious neurological process that occurs identically in all trained musicians regardless of cultural background.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It constitutes a form of subjectivity that is no less genuine for being involuntary and variable across individual listeners.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It has been demonstrated by controlled perceptual experiments to produce measurably greater emotional depth than Romantic compositional techniques.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is an artifact of poor compositional craft, arising only when the composer fails to supply adequate melodic material.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is most clearly illustrated in commercial ambient music, where the absence of structural complexity allows emergent figures to arise without distraction.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 describes emergent perception as involving 'phantom melodies, illusory accelerations, fleeting tonal centers' that the listener's nervous system produces — and the author calls the listener an 'involuntary co-author.' The passage argues this constitutes genuine subjectivity, not a lesser form of it. B synthesizes the involuntary nature and the variability ('differently each time') with the author's insistence that subjectivity is preserved.
explanations.A: The passage says the emergent figures arise 'differently each time,' implying individual variability; it does not claim the process is identical across listeners. Nor does it restrict emergent perception to trained musicians.
explanations.B: Correct. The passage calls the listener an 'involuntary co-author,' affirming that involuntary, variable emergent perception counts as genuine subjectivity — the core of the author's argument against the received view.
explanations.C: The passage does not appeal to controlled experiments; its argument is phenomenological and conceptual, not empirical.
explanations.D: This inverts the author's claim: emergent perception is presented as a sophisticated compositional achievement, not a failure of craft.
explanations.E: The passage explicitly distinguishes minimalism from ambient music on precisely this ground: ambient music produces 'stasis for consumption' and activates nothing emergent, while minimalism's lattice is 'designed to activate emergent perception.'

questions.questionStem: The author's reference to "standing inside a loom" (end of paragraph 2) functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: suggest that minimalist composers draw inspiration from craft and industrial processes rather than from the fine art tradition

choices.label: B
choices.text: illustrate the claim that the listener's perceptual participation completes the minimalist work rather than receiving it as a finished object

choices.label: C
choices.text: contrast the mechanical reproducibility of minimalist music with the unique, unrepeatable nature of Romantic performance

choices.label: D
choices.text: concede that minimalist music can feel impersonal and industrial, even if it ultimately achieves emotional depth

choices.label: E
choices.text: support the claim that minimalist repetition is derived from textile and weaving traditions in non-Western cultures

explanations.correct: The loom image immediately follows the claim that the listener perceives 'not a finished image but a process that one's own perceptual apparatus completes, differently each time.' The loom — a device whose output is produced by the interaction of its structure with the weaver's action — illustrates this co-completion idea. B identifies this exact rhetorical function.
explanations.A: The passage makes no claim about composers drawing from craft or industrial sources; the loom is a perceptual analogy, not a statement about compositional influences.
explanations.B: Correct. The loom is introduced to embody the contrast with 'watching a painting' (receiving a finished image) and to illustrate the listener's active, process-completing role.
explanations.C: The passage does not use the loom to contrast mechanical reproducibility with Romantic performance; reproducibility is never at issue in paragraph 2.
explanations.D: The loom image is not a concession — it is part of the author's positive account of minimalism's achievement, not an acknowledgment of a drawback.
explanations.E: The passage makes no reference to non-Western textile or weaving traditions anywhere; this is a plausible-sounding but entirely unsupported claim.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the author's central distinction between minimalist music and commercial ambient music?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several of Philip Glass's works were composed under commercial commissions and were subsequently used as background music in retail environments.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Listeners who are played minimalist works in laboratory settings consistently report lower emotional engagement than listeners who are played Romantic orchestral works.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Systematic studies of listeners' neural responses reveal that both canonical minimalist compositions and commercial ambient recordings reliably induce the emergence of phantom melodic figures in the auditory cortex.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some commercial ambient composers deliberately study and imitate the harmonic techniques of Glass and Reich in order to achieve a more sophisticated sonic texture.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Critics who initially dismissed minimalism as emotionally empty have, after repeated listening, revised their assessments upward.

explanations.correct: The author's central distinction rests on the claim that minimalism activates emergent perception in the listener while ambient music produces only 'stasis for consumption' offering 'nothing unexpected.' If empirical evidence showed that ambient music also reliably induces the same phantom-melody phenomenon in listeners' auditory cortices, the phenomenological distinction on which the entire argument turns would collapse. C directly attacks the mechanism the author identifies as decisive.
explanations.A: That Glass received commercial commissions and that some works were used as background music speaks to context of use, not to the phenomenological distinction the author draws between the two kinds of music's structural properties. This is off-target.
explanations.B: Lower reported emotional engagement with minimalism in laboratory settings might seem to support the critics the author is opposing, but the author's claim is about phenomenological density and the transfer of responsibility — not about what listeners self-report in artificial conditions. This is relevant but does not attack the central distinction between minimalism and ambient music specifically.
explanations.C: Correct. If ambient music also reliably activates emergent perception — the very mechanism the author treats as minimalism's distinguishing achievement — then the 'phenomenologically decisive' distinction the author draws dissolves.
explanations.D: That some ambient composers study Glass and Reich speaks only to influence, not to whether the resulting works achieve emergent perception. Imitation of harmonic technique does not establish that the phenomenological outcome is the same.
explanations.E: This actually supports the author's position — critics revising upward is consistent with the author's claim that repeated exposure reveals minimalism's depth. It does not undermine the distinction between minimalism and ambient music.
